name: Giorgio Parisi
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Parisi graduated in 1970 (age 22) and worked as a researcher at Frascati National Labs with published papers, but his landmark contributions—the Altarelli-Parisi (DGLAP) equations (1977), the KPZ equation (1985), and the Nobel Prize (2021)—all came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Parisi enrolled in physics at the University of Rome La Sapienza in 1966 and graduated in 1970 under Nicola Cabibbo. He then joined the Frascati National Laboratories as a researcher and spent a year at Columbia University (1973-74), publishing papers in particle physics, but had not yet produced a landmark result by age 26.
evidence_summary: Parisi earned his Laurea in physics from Sapienza in 1970 under Nicola Cabibbo and worked as a researcher at INFN's Frascati National Laboratories from 1971, with a visiting position at Columbia in 1973-74. While he had published scientific papers by age 26, his landmark contributions—the Altarelli-Parisi equations (1977), the exact solution of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model (1979-80), and the KPZ equation (1985)—all came after age 26. He received tenure at 27 and full professorship at 32, eventually winning the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics.

evidence_summary: Ruiz became the first person to earn a degree in astronomy from the University of Chile in 1971 at age 25, but this was a bachelor's-level qualification. name: E. C. George Sudarshan
milestone_by_age_26: Co-developed the V-A theory of weak interactions with Robert Marshak by December 1956–January 1957 at age 25, a fundamental contribution to particle physics that opened the way to the unified electroweak theory.
early_history_summary: Sudarshan showed early mathematical aptitude in school in Kerala, completed his B.Sc. (Honours) in Physics at Madras Christian College by age 20 (1951), and his MA at the University of Madras in 1952. He then spent three years as a research student at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research under Homi Bhabha and Bernard Peters before going to the University of Rochester in 1955 to work with Robert Marshak, where he systematically studied all weak interaction literature and by late 1956 concluded the interaction must be V-A.
family_context_summary: Born into a Syrian Christian family in Pallam, Kerala; father was a revenue supervisor for the Kerala government and mother was a school teacher. The family was middle-class but not wealthy.
parent_family_domain_summary: Neither parent had a background in physics or science; father was a government revenue supervisor and mother a school teacher. No domain advantage transferred.
primary_early_advantage_tags: TIFR research environment, Marshak mentorship, particle physics frontier, mathematical aptitude, Kerala outsider
evidence_summary: Sudarshan demonstrated early mathematical aptitude and completed his B.Sc. (Honours) in Physics at Madras Christian College by 1951 and his MA in 1952. He then spent three formative years as a research student at the elite Tata Institute of Fundamental Research under Homi Bhabha, gaining deep exposure to particle physics. At the University of Rochester with Robert Marshak, he systematically studied all weak interaction literature and by December 1956–January 1957, at age 25, concluded the universal weak interaction must be V-A—a fundamental result later vindicated by experiments and central to the electroweak theory. His mentorship under Marshak and the elite institutional pipeline (TIFR, Rochester) were key advantages.
starting_point: Born into a middle-class Syrian Christian family in Pallam, Kerala, India; father was a government revenue supervisor and mother a school teacher.
current_position: Died on 13 May 2018 in Austin, Texas at age 86; was Professor of Physics at the University of Texas at Austin and Director of the Center for Particle Physics.

trajectory.event: Joined the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Bombay as a research student under Homi Bhabha and Bernard Peters.
Moved to the University of Rochester to begin graduate studies under Robert Marshak.
Co-developed the V-A theory of weak interactions with Marshak, a fundamental result in particle physics.
Completed his PhD at the University of Rochester.

Joined the University of Texas at Austin as Professor of Physics and became Director of the Center for Particle Theory.
Awarded the Padma Bhushan, India's third-highest civilian honor.
Shared the ICTP Dirac Medal with Nicola Cabibbo for contributions to understanding weak interactions.
Died on 13 May 2018 in Austin, Texas.

name: Heinrich Messner

early_history_summary: Messner grew up in Obernberg am Brenner in Tyrol, the heart of Austrian alpine skiing country. He trained with Sportverein Tirol and rose through the Austrian skiing pipeline, winning his first national championship in downhill at age 22 in 1961 and adding slalom titles in 1964 and 1965.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Tyrol alpine skiing region, Austrian skiing pipeline, Sportverein Tirol, polyvalent skier
evidence_summary: Messner grew up in Obernberg am Brenner in Tyrol, Austria, a heartland of alpine skiing, which provided direct immersion in the sport from an early age. He trained with Sportverein Tirol and won his first Austrian national championship in downhill at age 22 in 1961, followed by slalom titles in 1964 and 1965. He competed at the 1964 Winter Olympics and later won the first World Cup race ever held in 1967, Olympic bronze medals in 1968 and 1972, and 16 World Cup podiums. His geographic immersion in the Tyrolean skiing ecosystem was the dominant early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Obernberg am Brenner, Tyrol, Austria, in the alpine skiing heartland; family background not documented in reviewed sources.

name: Alan Parker
milestone_by_age_26: Wrote the screenplay for the feature film 'Melody' (released 1971), his first produced film credit, while working as an advertising copywriter at age 26.
early_history_summary: Parker grew up in a working-class family on a council estate in Islington, North London, with no film industry connections. He left school at 18 to work in advertising, starting as an office boy at Ogilvy & Mather and rising to copywriter at agencies including Collett Dickenson Pearce, where he met future producers David Puttnam and Alan Marshall. He wrote hundreds of ads and directed commercials before Puttnam encouraged him to write his first film script, Melody, around 1969-1970.
family_context_summary: Born into a working-class family in Islington, North London; father was a house painter and mother a dressmaker. Grew up on a council estate with no aspirations to filmmaking and no family connections to the film industry.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family connection to film or media; father was a house painter, mother a dressmaker. An uncle inspired an early interest in photography.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Puttnam and Marshall collaboration, London advertising scene, working-class drive, prolific copywriting reps
evidence_summary: Parker grew up in a working-class Islington family with no film connections, but the London advertising scene of the 1960s provided a creative frontier. He wrote prolifically—over 300 ads in his first year—and met David Puttnam and Alan Marshall at Collett Dickenson Pearce, forming a high-trust peer team that would produce many of his films. Puttnam encouraged him to write his first screenplay, Melody (1971), which was produced when Parker was 26-27. His working-class background created urgency, and his advertising reps gave him storytelling and visual communication skills that transferred directly to filmmaking.
starting_point: Born into a working-class family on a council estate in Islington, North London; father was a house painter, mother a dressmaker, with no connections to the film industry.
current_position: Died on 31 July 2020 at age 76; was a knighted British film director, screenwriter, and producer known for films including Midnight Express, Fame, and Mississippi Burning.

trajectory.event: Wrote the screenplay for Melody, his first produced feature film, credited in Variety while still an advertising copywriter.
Directed The Evacuees for BBC, winning a BAFTA for Best Director and an International Emmy.

Directed Mississippi Burning, nominated for seven Academy Awards including Best Director.
Knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for services to the film industry.
Died on 31 July 2020 in London after a long illness.

name: Qasem Soleimani
milestone_by_age_26: Commanded the 41st Tharallah unit (initially a battalion, later expanded to brigade and division) of the IRGC during the Iran-Iraq War from 1980 at age 23, leading troops in combat across multiple fronts.
early_history_summary: Soleimani was born into an impoverished peasant family in Kerman Province, Iran. He left school at 13 to work on construction sites to repay his father's debts, later working as a technician for the Kerman Water Organization. After the 1979 Islamic Revolution, he joined the newly founded IRGC at age 22, quickly became an instructor, and by 1980 was commanding the 41st Tharallah unit on the Iran-Iraq War front lines.
family_context_summary: Born into an impoverished peasant family in the village of Qanat-e Malek, Kerman Province; father was a small-time farmer who fell into debt due to the Shah's land reform. Soleimani left school at 13 to work in construction to help repay approximately $100 in agricultural debt.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family military or political background; father was a small-time farmer. The family's poverty and the father's debt crisis forced early labor and bred resentment toward the Shah's regime.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Islamic Revolution structural wave, IRGC elite corps, poverty-driven urgency, frontline combat immersion, physical fitness
evidence_summary: Soleimani rose from extreme poverty in rural Kerman Province, leaving school at 13 to repay his father's debts through construction labor. The 1979 Islamic Revolution was a massive structural wave that created the IRGC, which he joined at 22 with minimal training but quickly became an instructor. By 1980, at age 23, he was commanding the 41st Tharallah unit on the Iran-Iraq War front lines, leading troops through almost every major operation of the eight-year war. His adversity-driven urgency, physical fitness from weight training, and direct combat immersion were the defining factors of his early rise. He later commanded the Quds Force from 1998 until his assassination by the US in 2020.
starting_point: Born into an impoverished peasant family in Qanat-e Malek, Kerman Province, Iran; father was a small-time farmer burdened by debt from the Shah's land reform.
current_position: Assassinated by US drone strike on 3 January 2020 in Baghdad, Iraq at age 62; was commander of the Quds Force, described as the most powerful operative in the Middle East.

trajectory.event: Joined the newly founded IRGC after the Islamic Revolution and quickly became an instructor of new recruits.
Took command of the 41st Tharallah unit at the start of the Iran-Iraq War, leading troops from Kerman Province.
The 41st Tharallah unit was expanded to a full division under his command, with three infantry brigades and one armored battalion.
Participated in the climactic expedition to the al-Faw Peninsula as the Iran-Iraq War ended.
Appointed commander of the Quds Force, the IRGC division responsible for extraterritorial and clandestine military operations.
Played a key role in securing Russian military intervention in the Syrian civil war.
Assassinated by a US drone strike ordered by President Trump on 3 January 2020 in Baghdad, Iraq.

name: Johan Galtung
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; Galtung earned his cand. real. in mathematics in 1956 (age 26) and co-authored his first book 'Gandhi's Political Ethics' with Arne Naess at age 24, but his landmark achievements—founding PRIO (1959), establishing the Journal of Peace Research (1964), and the world's first peace studies chair (1969)—all came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Galtung was born in Oslo and experienced WWII under German occupation, seeing his father arrested by Nazis. By 1951 he was a committed peace mediator, doing 18 months of social service instead of military service and spending 6 months in prison as a conscientious objector at age 24, during which he co-authored his first book with Arne Naess. He earned his cand. real. in mathematics in 1956 and mag. art. in sociology in 1957, both from the University of Oslo.
family_context_summary: Born in Oslo, Norway; father was a physician who also studied political economy and attended the Norwegian Military Academy, serving as deputy mayor. Father was imprisoned by Nazis during WWII, which had a lasting effect on Galtung.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a multi-disciplinary scholar (medicine, military tactics, political economy) and politician; his broad intellectual approach influenced Galtung's own multi-disciplinary path in mathematics and sociology.
evidence_summary: Galtung earned his cand. real. in mathematics at the University of Oslo in 1956 at age 26 and co-authored 'Gandhi's Political Ethics' with philosopher Arne Naess while imprisoned as a conscientious objector at age 24. However, his landmark achievements—founding the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO) in 1959 at age 29, establishing the Journal of Peace Research in 1964, and being appointed to the world's first chair in peace and conflict studies in 1969—all came after age 26. While the co-authored book is independently verifiable, his fame and field-defining contributions arrived later.

name: Viktor Zinger
milestone_by_age_26: Won World Championship gold medals with the Soviet national team in 1965, 1966, and 1967 (ages 23-25), and the Soviet league title with Spartak Moscow in 1967, establishing himself as a key goaltender in the dominant Soviet hockey system.
early_history_summary: Zinger started playing hockey with CSKA Moscow in 1958 at age 17 under legendary coach Anatoly Tarasov, but could not break into the top goaltender position. He moved to SKA Kuibyshev in 1961 for four seasons of regular play, then joined HC Spartak Moscow in 1964, which led to his selection for the Soviet national team in 1965 and a string of World Championship gold medals.
primary_early_advantage_tags: CSKA Moscow under Tarasov, Spartak Moscow, Soviet national team, Soviet hockey dominance, butterfly goaltending style
evidence_summary: Zinger entered the elite Soviet hockey pipeline at 17, training under legendary coach Anatoly Tarasov at CSKA Moscow from 1958. After gaining regular playing experience at SKA Kuibyshev (1961-64), he joined Spartak Moscow in 1964 and was selected for the Soviet national team in 1965. He won World Championship gold medals in 1965, 1966, 1967, and 1969, Olympic gold in 1968, and Soviet league titles in 1967, 1969, and 1976. The Soviet sports system provided elite training, infrastructure, and competitive immersion from a young age. He was inducted into the Russian and Soviet Hockey Hall of Fame in 1967 and served as backup to Tretiak in the 1972 Summit Series.
starting_point: Born in Davydovo, USSR; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died on 24 September 2013 in Moscow at age 71; had retired from playing in 1977 and served as a longtime goaltender coach and junior team coach with Spartak Moscow.
